newsitem.title: UK: Car explodes in Belfast as Blair warns Sinn Fein.
newsitem.headline: Car explodes in Belfast as Blair warns Sinn Fein.

text.p: A car exploded in central Belfast on Saturday, injuring three people, as British Prime Minister Tony Blair told the IRA not to delay a new truce to get its Sinn Fein spokesmen invited to peace talks.
Some witnesses said armed British troops had surrounded the vehicle in the usually peaceful University area of Belfast when it exploded and caught fire, shattering windows.
"I was in my office and a heard a bang and I looked out of the window and saw a car in flames," an eyewitness, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.

Police said three people were injured, none seriously, and some witnesses said they believed three or four men in the vehicle may have been hurt in the blast. There was no immediate confirmation that the blast was caused by a bomb. It would be the first in Belfast this year. Police said they were not questioning anyone at present.

It occured as Blair voiced impatience at the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which killed two soldiers in Lurgan last Monday shortly after British government officials renewed contact with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein.

Blair told reporters in Denver, where he is attending the Group of Seven summit, that he would not wait for ever for the IRA to call a halt to its 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland. He urged the guerrillas to renew a broken 17-month ceasefire which could allow Sinn Fein to take part in year-old Belfast negotiations on a settlement between pro-British Protestants and pro-Irish Catholics. "The people of Northern Ireland have got the right to expect the government to push this process forward with or without Sinn Fein -- so the ball is in their court," he said.
Blair is expected to spell out his newly-elected government's position in Northern Ireland in a major statement to parliament on Wednesday.
Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, earlier on Saturday rejected Blair's criticism over the IRA killings in Lurgan.
"No good will ever come of the current efforts to blame Sinn Fein for recent killings. Short-termism has never worked in the past. Peace-making is a difficult business," Adams said.
He was responding to Blair's remarks on his way to Denver in which he voiced outrage at the IRA's double killing, staged after Britain lifted a ban on contact with Sinn Fein.
Adams, in a statement issued in Belfast, said Blair's government had to remove what he called "obstacles created by the last government" to its entry to the year-old Belfast talks.
The Sinn Fein leader said the main stumbling block was so-called "decommissioning", the surrender of IRA arms.

"To do this absolute clarity is required. Especially on the issue of decommissioning. Decommissioning has not yet been removed as an obstacle in the negotiations. This remains the biggest stumbling block," Adams said.

Blair is expected to throw some light on the issue on Wednesday after consulting U.S. President Bill Clinton and his Irish partners in a three-year attempt to find a negotiated settlement to the conflict, which has killed 3,200.

The two governments lifted a ban on official contacts with Sinn Fein to hold exploratory talks on its demand to be included in the negotiations but reimposed the sanction after the two killings by IRA hit-men in Lurgan last Monday.
The IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February last year after it failed to be admitted to the negotiations because of demands that the IRA show willing to give up its arsenal.
